transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood Solution Architect), Mark Davison (Atlas Retail - Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Atlas - Platform Eng), Alan Wu (Atlas - SRE), Priya Singh (Atlas - Data Platform)

Summary (auto): SE walked through recommended OpenTelemetry spans/metrics for per-token observability. Customers asked about noise, sampling, storage, and how to map token-level traces to SLOs. Action items captured below.

Topics: OpenTelemetry schema, token-level metrics, per-token span design, batching attribution, KV cache hit tagging, quantization telemetry, dashboards, VPC collector options, security and PII concerns.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, welcome thanks for joining. today we did the intake, now priya will run through the deep dive on otel and token metrics.
[00:12] Priya: thanks jordan hi team, i'm priya nair from redwood, i'm going to jump into how we instrument the runtime so you can see per-token timings, kv-cache hits, batching latency and model kernel time. i'll call out a few caveats up front — some transcriptions may show O T E L spelled O-T-E-L or otel, you'll see the same in our examples.
[00:34] Mark: great, our main concern is we need per-token latency so product can alert when median token time spikes; also we need to know whether it's the network, batching, or model.
[00:46] Priya: totally, and that maps to three broad categories of spans and metrics: network/request ingress, runtime orchestration (batching + kv cache), and model execution (kernel time, quantized kernels). we recommend emitting both traces (spans) for sampled requests and high-cardinality metrics for rollups.
[01:10] Alan: quick question — do you recommend instrumenting every token as a span? that sounds high volume.
[01:18] Priya: right, don't create a span per token in the tracing system at full sampling; instead we do hybrid: emit per-token counters and timing histograms to metrics (Prometheus/OTLP metrics) and create sampled traces that contain per-token annotations for a small fraction, e.g., 1% or 0.1% depending on QPS. that gives you both precise distributions and deep root-cause for individual requests.
[01:40] Sofia: can you elaborate on the metrics names/labels? we worry about cardinality with things like model_version, quantization_profile, route etc.
[01:49] Priya: yes, keep metric labels limited: service, model_family, model_version (coarse), deployment_tier (hosted/dedicated), batch_size_bucket, kv_cache_hit (true/false), quant_profile (q4_q8 etc). don't put user ids or complete prompt text. for traces we add higher-cardinality attributes only on sampled traces.
[02:13] Carlos: also note the runtime emits a per-token timing metric we call redwood_token_duration_seconds (histogram) and a counter redwood_token_count, plus redwood_batching_wait_seconds for time spent waiting to batch. these are exported via OTLP/Prometheus.
[02:33] Mark: is redwood_token_duration_seconds broken down to micro-ops? like preproc, cache lookup, kv cache serialization?
[02:40] Priya: we break the timeline into stages: ingress parsing, prefix/KV lookup, batching wait, kernel execution, post-processing (e.g., function-calling/structuring). kernel execution itself can be split into kv cache read (local), kv cache fetch (if miss and remote), and compute. some labels may say 'kv_cache_hit' and an attribute kv_cache_source=local|remote.
[03:05] Mark: ok that helps. about kv cache, how do we attribute latency when a cache miss triggers upstream fetch?
[03:13] Priya: we include span joins: the request span will have a child span for kv lookup which will indicate hit/miss. on miss, there will be additional spans for remote fetch; sampling ensures you'd see full waterfall on sampled traces. metrics will increment redwood_kv_miss_count and tag with model & route so you can alert. be mindful of cardinality on route.
[03:40] Alan: for our VPC deployment we can't send traces out to SaaS; what are options?
[03:45] Priya: two options: 1) run an OTEL collector inside your VPC that exports to your Prometheus/Grafana or to a local OTLP endpoint; or 2) send aggregated metrics only, keep traces on-prem. Redwood Private can forward metrics to your observability stack via secure peering and you can ship logs/traces to your S3/KMS bucket for longer term. we'll share a sample collector config.
[04:12] Sofia: any notes on auth/PII? we can't have prompt text in traces.
[04:18] Priya: absolutely — never include prompt text or user PII as attributes. We provide sanitized attributes: prompt_id, prompt_length, but never content. For private clusters you can configure scrubbing and redaction at the collector level.
[04:35] Jordan: can you walk through an example trace and corresponding dashboard?
[04:40] Priya: yes, example: a trace starts at request ingress span (~10ms), then batching wait span (~40ms if unsatisfied batch), token loop where we record token metrics aggregate (we emit histogram buckets per token), kv-lookup child span (5ms hit or 120ms remote fetch), kernel execution span (varies by model/quantization, e.g., 18ms q8 vs 40ms fp32), and finalization span. On the dashboard we show per-token p50/p95 histograms, batch wait distribution, kv hit ratio over time, kernel execution heatmap by model_version.
[05:20] Mark: what about quantization — will metrics change?
[05:24] Priya: kernel time will change and you should add quant_profile label. Quantized runs often reduce kernel time but may increase CPU work for dequant, so include exec_cpu_seconds and exec_gpu_ms as separate metrics. Also track model output quality separately — not part of observability but essential for rollouts.
[05:46] Carlos: note that quantization can change memory access patterns and KV cache serialization; labels help attribute.
[05:54] Sofia: sampling strategy — 1% traces ok? our QPS is 2k rps so 1% is 720 traces per hour — is that too much?
[06:05] Priya: it depends on retention and size; sampling should be adaptive. Start with error and p99-triggered full traces: keep head-based sampling for slow requests and random sampling for normal traffic. Use tail-sampling for traces that hit certain error conditions or latency thresholds.
[06:29] Alan: storing token-level histograms at high resolution will be heavy in prometheus. suggestions?
[06:35] Priya: push histograms with coarse buckets and summarize: e.g., <1ms, 1-5ms, 5-15ms, 15-50ms, 50-200ms, >200ms. Downsample or roll up high-resolution buckets into hourly aggregates for long-term storage, or send to a metrics backend that supports histograms natively.
[06:58] Mark: what about end-to-end SLO alerting? we want alert when per-response generation latency exceeds X or token p95 jumps.
[07:06] Priya: define SLOs at two levels: request-level (generation latency <= 300ms p95) and token-level (token p95 <= 30ms). Create alerts on sudden shifts in token p95 and on batching wait increases. Also use anomaly detection over token histograms.
[07:32] Sofia: are there prebuilt dashboards?
[07:35] Priya: yes we'll share Grafana dashboards: overview (throughput, latency, error rate), token-inspector (per-token p50/p95, heatmap), batching and queue lengths, kv cache health (hit rate, miss latency), model kernel timings by model_version and quant_profile.
[07:55] Mark: can you show the sample OTLP collector config?
[07:59] Priya: sure — high level: collector receives OTLP/gRPC from runtime, processors: resource detection, batch, probabilistic sampler for traces, then exporters: OTLP to your local telemetry, and Prometheus exporter for metrics scraping. We'll include config in the follow-up.
[08:22] Carlos: caveat: when running in Private on-prem with no external internet, ensure collector has access to local Prometheus or a partner endpoint; we support pushing to S3 as well.
[08:36] Alan: you mentioned high-cardinality attributes on traces; any guardrails?
[08:41] Priya: yes, enforce attribute allow-lists and use hashing for sensitive keys, avoid user ids, and cap unique values per minute. The collector can drop or hash attributes.
[08:58] Mark: how about correlating tokens to business metrics like revenue per generation?
[09:03] Priya: add route or feature flags as low-card labels, then join with business metrics in your BI. We avoid embedding business ids in high-cardinality telemetry.
[09:18] Sofia: operational question: if we enable token-level metrics, what's expected ingestion volume?
[09:24] Priya: depends on QPS and token count; e.g., 2k rps with avg 30 tokens => 60k token events per second. If you only emit aggregated histograms per request you reduce cardinality considerably. We'll help model the math for your traffic.
[09:45] Mark: we want to run a benchmark. what does redwood need from us?
[09:49] Jordan: ideal: sample trace payloads, peak QPS target, desired model (e.g., vicuna-13b-q4), and whether we should run hosted or dedicated. We'll provision a trial dedicated for the run.
[10:03] Priya: For the benchmark we'll also recommend enabling kv cache with both local and remote paths so we can exercise miss/hit ratios. Instrumentation will run during the benchmark to show waterfall charts.
[10:18] Alan: any note about encryption and KMS for telemetry? we require keys managed by our KMS.
[10:24] Priya: in Private deployments you can route telemetry through your collector which has access to your KMS and forward to S3 encrypted. For hosted scenarios, we provide options to push metrics only and keep traces on-prem. We'll share architecture diagrams.
[10:38] Sofia: are there examples of alert rules for kv miss spikes?
[10:42] Priya: yes, e.g., alert when kv_miss_rate > 5% and miss_latency_p95 > 200ms for 5 minutes. Another rule: batch_wait_p95 > 100ms for 3 minutes.
[10:56] Mark: curious about interplay between batching and latency — sometimes batching lowers cost but raises p95; how to visualize tradeoff?
[11:03] Priya: we surface batch_size_bucket vs p50/p95 kernel time. Also show cost estimate per 1M tokens for different batching configs. For production you can set dynamic batching based on latency SLOs: target lower batch sizes during peak latency and auto-burst when latency is fine.
[11:28] Carlos: we also capture queuing metrics per infer worker so you can identify hot shards.
[11:33] Sofia: can we correlate with hardware level metrics (GPU utilization, memory pressure)?
[11:36] Priya: yes, we emit host metrics and GPU metrics as part of the same collector pipeline; join by deployment/instance id. That helps identify if kernel slowdown is due to GPU saturation or memory thrashing.
[11:52] Alan: any gotchas in Prometheus scrape for histograms?
[11:56] Priya: Prometheus histograms must be designed carefully; prefer summary metrics for percentiles at ingestion time if your backend supports it. For Prometheus, use stable bucket boundaries and avoid creating new high-card buckets dynamically.
[12:12] Mark: safety and PII again — confirm no raw prompt text ever leaves runtime.
[12:17] Priya: correct — runtime strips text from telemetry and only emits metadata. we will provide redaction configs.
[12:25] Jordan: can we talk about concrete dashboard fields you'll share?
[12:29] Priya: yes: throughput (rps), tokens per second, redwood_token_duration_seconds p50/p95, redwood_batching_wait_seconds p50/p95, redwood_kv_hit_ratio, kernel_latency_by_model_version, quant_profile_breakdown, error_rate, failed_span_count. We'll include templated Grafana JSON panels.
[12:55] Mark: how do you suggest we onboard this without flooding our monitoring?
[12:59] Priya: phased approach: stage 1 — metrics only (coarse histograms, kv tags, batch wait), stage 2 — enable sampled traces with tail sampling on errors/slow requests, stage 3 — add advanced dashboards and SLO alerting.
[13:18] Sofia: what's the expected CPU overhead of collector on each node?
[13:22] Priya: small; collector cost is modest vs runtime. If you choose to emit per-token high-card metrics it can increase CPU and network. Prefer local aggregation in the collector before export.
[13:36] Alan: will Redwood provide prebuilt OTEL semantic conventions?
[13:39] Priya: yes, we publish semantic conventions for spans and metric names. We'll share the doc and a proto file for instrumentation.
[13:48] Mark: any example queries we can use in Grafana to detect regressions?
[13:53] Priya: queries like: increase(redwood_token_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) / increase(redwood_token_count[5m]) to compute p50-ish approximations; and rate(redwood_kv_miss_count[5m]) / rate(redwood_kv_request_count[5m]) for miss ratio. We'll send ready-to-go queries.
[14:19] Jordan: let's pivot to VPC and private constraints — particularly collector placement and secure export.
[14:24] Priya: place collector in same VPC subnet as runtime, configure to export internally to your metrics stack, and limit egress. For Private we support sidecar collector or centralized collector per VPC. Use MTLS for OTLP exporters and integrate with your KMS for credentials.
[14:46] Carlos: for air-gapped environments we recommend storing trace artifacts to S3 on the private network and optionally ship compressed bundles to a secure offline analysis cluster.
[14:58] Mark: anything specific about on-prem GPUs and kernel metric collection?
[15:03] Priya: install GPU exporters (NVIDIA DCGM) and ensure collector scrapes those. We map GPU metrics to inference job ids. kernel metrics are correlated by deployment instance tag.
[15:17] Sofia: can we instrument quantization toggles per rollout?
[15:20] Priya: yes, include quant_profile label and version in metrics so you can compare kernel time and quality across rollout cohorts.
[15:30] Alan: talk about storage retention — how long should we keep token histograms?
[15:34] Priya: short-term high-res (7-14 days), long-term rollups (90 days+) for trend analysis. full traces usually 7-30 days depending on storage.
[15:46] Mark: okay any risks we should be mindful of?
[15:50] Priya: watch for runaway cardinality, PII leakage, and sampling misconfig. Also ensure your alerting thresholds are based on baseline traffic windows to avoid noise.
[16:04] Jordan: wrapping up — quick recap and next steps?
[16:08] Mark: yes please.
[16:10] Priya: recap: we'll share OTEL collector config, Grafana dashboards, metric names/semantics, and a benchmark plan. Pilot will use Dedicated with kv cache enabled. Atlas to send sample traffic and current Prometheus targets.
[16:25] Jordan: action items — we'll email docs and set up the benchmark week. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (OTEL spelled different ways, KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash). Some speaker labeling may be approximate.
